newsitem.title: USA: Beaufort Sea oil lease sale draws $14.4 million.
newsitem.headline: Beaufort Sea oil lease sale draws $14.4 million.

text.p: Alaska's first outercontinental shelf oil and gas lease sale in five years drew a total $14.4 million in high bids, according to preliminary figures released by the U.S. Minerals Management Service Wednesday.
Bids were opened Wednesday morning for Lease Sale 144, which had offered 7.3 million offshore acres in Arctic Alaska's Beaufort Sea.
Twenty-nine bidding units received a total 31 bids, MMS officials said.
The largest bid came from British Petroleum unit BP Exploration (Alaska) Inc., which offered $10.6 million for a single segment near the existing Tern unit north of Prudhoe Bay.
BP also won several other tracts in the area.
Other bidders were Atlantic Richfield unit Arco Alaska Inc., Anardarko, Chevron and Petrofina Delaware.
Arco, in partnership with Anadarko, won tracts north of the federally owned National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska and about 120 miles east of Prudhoe Bay.
Bidding alone, Arco won tracts near the Colville River Delta and in Camden Bay, areas where the company has already conducted exploration.
BP and Petrofina, bidding separately, won tracts directly north of Prudhoe Bay. Petrofina's bids were for tracts near the existing Sandpiper unit on the North Slope.
Chevron won tracts west of Prudhoe Bay and north of the Colville Delta.
Interior Department officials at the lease sale were pleased with the results.
"I do think it's an encouraging showing," said Cynthia Quarterman, director of the U.S. Minerals Management Service, who attended the sale as part of an Alaska trip.
Industry interest in the area was muted in past years because of high operating costs and disappointing exploration results.
But BP's recent successes at its offshore Northstar prospect, which straddles state and federal leases, may have inspired other companies to return to the Beaufort Sea, Quarterman said.
"Technology must have improved in the last five years to make people think these will be economic in the next 10 years," she said.
Also encouraged was Ken Boyd, director of the Alaska Division of Oil and Gas.
The state will receive a 27 percent share of bid proceeds for most of the leased tracts, which are located within six miles of shore, he said.

More important for the state, the federal lease sale indicates renewed interest in Alaska development by Chevron, which a few years ago halted its North SLope operations and shut down its Anchorage office, and industry interest in some new sites, Boyd said.
"I'm glad to see Chevron back," said Boyd, who attended the sale.

The state has a North Slope lease sale scheduled for October 1. That sale will comprise acreage around the Colville Delta and will include some acreage owned by Barrow-based Arctic Slope Regional Corp., an Inupiat Eskimo regional corporation.
